p: `1→2→3→4→5`, `k = 2`. Counting gives `n = 5`, tail = 5, `k %= n` leaves `k = 2`.

blocks.h: Why `k %= n` and why the early return when `k == 0`?
p: Without the modulo, large k would walk around the ring many times. If `k % n == 0` the code would otherwise compute `range(n - 1)`, reach the tail, set `tail.next = None` and reconnect it to head: harmless here, but the early return avoids needless work.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass to find the length and tail, one partial pass to the cut point.
Space: O(1) — only pointers.

61.takeaway: Rotate a list by making it a ring: find the length, reduce k modulo n, cut after the (n−k)-th node.

DP transition for 'only right or down' moves

p: `[[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]]`. Each cell becomes its own cost plus the cheaper of the cumulative sums above and to the left. Final grid: [[1, 4, 5], [2, 7, 6], [6, 8, 7]].

In row 0 there is no cell above, and in column 0 no cell to the left. Reading `grid[i-1][j]` with `i = 0` would silently use the last row (Python negative indexing), giving wrong answers rather than an error. `inf` makes the missing side lose every `min`, so row 0 and column 0 only accumulate along the edge.

Because moves are only right or down, any path to a cell must come from directly above or directly left. The best path to a cell is its cost plus the best path to one of those two. Greedy choices at each step would fail; the DP compares complete cumulative costs.

bullets: Time: O(m·n) — each cell once.
Space: O(1) extra, since the input grid is overwritten (use a copy if the input must be preserved).

64.takeaway: Grid DP with two incoming directions: dp[i][j] = cost + min(from above, from left), reusing the grid as the table.

Base cases of the recurrence ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2)
n−1 updates move `b` from step 1 up to step n
For n = 1 the loop doesn't run and the answer is 1
Simultaneous assignment: the right side is computed with the old values

p: `n = 5` needs 4 updates. `b` is always the number of ways to reach the current step, so the answer is 8:

The last move onto step i was either a 1-step from i−1 or a 2-step from i−2, and the two groups never overlap. So ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2), the Fibonacci recurrence. Storing only the last two values removes the O(n) array.
Writing `a = b; b = a + b` would make the second line use the new `a`, giving `b + b`. The tuple form `a, b = b, a + b` evaluates the right side first, so `a + b` uses the old values.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass.
Space: O(1) — two variables.

70.takeaway: 1-D DP compressed to two rolling values: ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2), the Fibonacci pattern.

p: `s = 'ADOBECODEBANC'`, `t = 'ABC'`. The window `[l, r]` expands with `r`; while it covers all of `t`, it shrinks from the left. Selected steps (the rest only expand):

Counts below 0 mean we already have enough of that letter (or it is not in `t` at all, such as `D`, `O`, `E`). Only a letter still needed (> 0) moves us closer to covering `t`. In the shrink loop the mirror test `need[s[l]] > 0` after adding back detects that removing this letter made the window incomplete again, so the loop stops.

blocks.h: Why a `while` loop for the left edge?
p: After one new character, the window can often shrink by several positions while still covering `t` (at `r = 12` it shrinks from `l = 8` to `l = 10`, improving the best to `BANC`). An `if` would skip all but one shrink and miss the minimum.

bullets: Time: O(n + m) — each pointer only moves forward; each character is added once and removed at most once.
Space: O(k) for the counter, where k is the number of distinct characters.
If no window ever covers `t`, `best` keeps `inf` and the code returns `''`.

76.takeaway: Sliding window with a need-count: expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left as far as it stays valid, tracking the shortest.

blocks.h: Why does `prev` move only in the `else` branch?
p: `prev` must always point at the last node known to stay in the answer. After removing a duplicate run we don't yet know whether the next node is unique (it might start another run), so `prev` stays put and `prev.next` is re-pointed instead. Space: O(1) — pointers only.

82.takeaway: Dummy head plus a `prev` pointer that trails the last kept node lets you delete whole runs of duplicates in one pass.

p: Matrix `10100 / 10111 / 11111 / 10010`. After each row we have a histogram `h`; the monotonic stack finds the largest rectangle under it. Areas computed at pops:

blocks.h: Why does this reduce to 'largest rectangle in a histogram'?
p: A rectangle of 1s in the grid has its bottom edge on some row. Seen from that row, each column's consecutive 1s above form a bar, and the rectangle is a set of adjacent bars cut at the shortest one. Doing the histogram problem once per row covers every possible bottom edge.

Equal heights are popped too, so the remaining bar extends the width to the left. Equal bars on the stack would give correct final answers anyway, but popping them keeps strictly increasing heights and avoids duplicate work.

bullets: Time: O(m·n) — per row, each of n+1 indexes is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n) for `h` and the stack.

85.takeaway: Row-by-row histogram heights plus a monotonic stack: the largest rectangle of 1s is the best histogram rectangle over all bottom rows.
